title: 2025 is the Year of Evals! Just like 2024, and 2023, and … — John Dickerson, CEO Mozilla AI

summary: John Dickerson introduces himself as co-founder and chief scientist at Arthur AI (six years) before becoming CEO of Mozilla AI, which builds open source AI tooling. His central thesis: ML monitoring and evaluation are two sides of the same ruler—observability requires measurement, the core of evaluation. For years this was not a C-suite concern. Three concurrent forces now change that: ChatGPT made AI legible to CEOs, CFOs, and CISOs; a recession-driven budget freeze funneled discretionary enterprise spend toward GenAI; and agentic systems now act autonomously rather than merely feeding inputs into larger systems. Pre-ChatGPT, ML monitoring existed (H2O, Algorithmia, Seldon, Arise, Arthur, Galileo, Fiddler) but had tenuous links to business KPIs; selling required dollars-saved stories and deals stalled at the CIO level. Every VC pitch deck since the mid-2010s predicted a CEO firing over an ML screw-up that never materialized. JPMC spent only $100M on AIML from 2017–2021. ChatGPT launched Nov 30, 2022, unlocking discretionary GenAI budgets. 2023 became science-project year; 2024 saw GenAI apps reach production drawing governance scrutiny; 2025 shows scaled revenue and autonomous agents. Dickerson then defines agents per late-1950s literature: they perceive, learn, abstract, generalize, reason, and act—introducing complexity and risk ideal for the eval space. He maps the full C-suite: CEOs now understand capabilities and allocate budget; CFOs need quantitative eval numbers for spreadsheets; CISOs, faster and scrappier than CIOs, write checks for guardrail products addressing hallucination, prompt injection, and security; CIOs and CTOs want standards and numbers. All are now aligned on evaluation need. The industry has shifted to multi-agent systems monitoring—monitoring the whole system, not just one model. Leaked revenue numbers from The Information (mid-April, lagged 6–8 months) understate current eval startup revenues. Mozilla offers a non-monetized open-source project called any agent for multi-agent frameworks. In Q&A, Dickerson addresses domain expertise: experts cost $50–$200/hour via platforms like Merkur, sitting alongside multi-agent systems for human validation; dataset and environment creation can become a competitive moat. On LLMs-as-judges, he notes they solve dataset creation problems as a poor man's human judge but carry biases documented in an ICLR paper, requiring validation.

takeaways: Monitoring/observability and evaluation are inseparable: you cannot monitor without measuring, and measurement is the core function of evaluation.
Three forces make 2025 the year of evals: C-suite AI literacy post-ChatGPT, recession-frozen budgets channeled into GenAI, and agentic systems acting autonomously.
For a decade ML monitoring companies struggled because they could not connect model performance to downstream business KPIs that C-suite buyers care about.
Every VC pitch deck since the mid-2010s predicted a CEO firing over an ML incident; it still has not happened.
ChatGPT's launch in Nov 2022 unlocked discretionary GenAI budgets that otherwise would have been frozen by recession fears.
The adoption arc: 2023 = GenAI science projects, 2024 = internal production apps with governance questions, 2025 = scaled deployments and autonomous agents.
The full C-suite—CEO, CFO, CISO, CIO, CTO—is now aligned on evaluation; CISOs write checks fastest for guardrail products.
Industry has shifted to monitoring entire multi-agent systems, not just individual models.
Domain expertise in evals is addressed via expensive human validation ($50–$200/hour experts); dataset and environment creation can become a competitive moat.
LLMs-as-judges solve dataset creation problems but carry documented biases requiring human validation.

sections.title: Introduction: Arthur AI, Mozilla AI, and the Thesis
sections.summary: Dickerson introduces his background at Arthur AI (observability, evaluation, security across traditional ML, deep learning, GenAI, and agentic AI) and Mozilla AI's open source mission. He states his thesis: monitoring and evaluation are two sides of the same ruler; measurement is core to both.

sections.title: Three Forces Making 2025 the Year of Evals
sections.summary: Three concurrent forces drive evaluation to C-suite prominence: non-technical executives understanding AI after ChatGPT, recession-fear budget freezes channeling spend into GenAI pet projects, and agentic systems acting autonomously. Companies like Brain Trust, Arthur, Arise AI, and Galileo are seeing big takeoff.

sections.title: Year of the Agent and Historical ML Opacity
sections.summary: Agents now make decisions and take complex actions semi-autonomously. Previously, ML outputs were ingested into opaque systems, burying the need for evals below the CIO level. The need for evaluation was not obvious to the full C-suite.

sections.title: Pre-ChatGPT ML Monitoring Landscape
sections.summary: Before ChatGPT, ML monitoring existed (H2O, Algorithmia, Seldon, Arise, Arthur, Galileo, Fiddler, plus Snowflake, Databricks, Datadog, SageMaker, Vertex) but had tenuous links to business KPIs. Selling required dollars-saved stories. Every VC pitch deck predicted a CEO firing over ML—never happened. Security and latency always outranked model quality as priorities.

sections.title: JPMC Example and VC Predictions
sections.summary: Jamie Dimon's April 2022 annual report showed JPMC invested $100M in AIML from 2017–2021, comically small for a bank that size. Forward-thinking leaders existed but spending remained modest. The CEO-firing prediction remained unfulfilled.

sections.title: Macroeconomic Backdrop and Budget Freeze
sections.summary: Late 2022 recession fears caused enterprises to freeze or shrink 2023 IT budgets. Without the ChatGPT tailwind, little new technology spending would have occurred in enterprise IT departments in 2023.

sections.title: ChatGPT Launch and Budget Unlock
sections.summary: ChatGPT launched Nov 30, 2022, before holidays. Dickerson was at a NeurIPS event with Index Ventures that night. The wow factor—CEOs, CFOs, and non-technical users interacting easily with a single UI—unlocked discretionary budgets specifically for GenAI pet projects.

sections.title: 2023–2025: Science Projects to Scaled Autonomy
sections.summary: 2023: austerity continued but all new spend went to GenAI science projects. 2024: GenAI apps (internal chat, hiring tools) entered production; business-suit stakeholders began asking about ROI, governance, risk, compliance, brand optics. 2025: scaled revenue, large real AI budgets, technology improvements, and autonomous agents make evaluation unavoidable.

sections.title: Agent Definition and System-Level Complexity
sections.summary: Dickerson defines agents per late-1950s literature: they perceive the environment, learn, abstract, generalize, reason, and act. Unlike traditional ML, reasoning models and systems acting in virtual or cyber-physical environments introduce significant complexity and risk—great for the eval/observability space.

sections.title: Connecting Evals to Business KPIs and Full C-Suite Alignment
sections.summary: Selling any product requires attaching it to downstream business KPIs: risk mitigation, revenue gains, losing less money. Evaluations quantify these and are finally first-class discussion points. CEOs now understand GenAI and agentic capabilities and allocate budget. CFOs need quantitative eval numbers for budget spreadsheets. CISOs—scrappier and faster check-writers than CIOs—buy guardrail products for hallucination detection and prompt injection. CIOs and CTOs want standards and data-driven decisions. The full C-suite is now aligned on evaluation need.

sections.title: Multi-Agent Systems Monitoring and Revenue Trajectory
sections.summary: All eval/observability/monitoring/security companies have shifted to multi-agent systems monitoring—monitoring the whole system, not just one model used by one agent. Leaked revenue numbers from The Information (mid-April) for startups like Galileo and Brain Trust were lagged 6–8 months and no longer representative. Dickerson predicts 2026 leaks may finally show revenue no longer lagging at AI eval startups.

sections.title: Mozilla's Any Agent Open Source Project
sections.summary: Mozilla is not firmly in the eval space but offers any agent, a non-monetized open-source project implementing multiple multi-agent system frameworks under a unified interface for experimentation.

sections.title: Q&A: Domain Expertise in Evaluations
sections.summary: Asked how domain expertise (e.g., DCF analysis) is incorporated into evals, Dickerson references his Nature Machine Intelligence paper on persona-based agent limitations. A leaked Merkur spreadsheet shows experts at $50–$200/hour hired by Google, Meta, and banks for human validation alongside multi-agent systems. Dataset and environment creation can become a competitive moat, as the investment capital into specialized eval environments differentiates versus competitors.

sections.title: Q&A: LLMs as Judges
sections.summary: Dickerson addresses the LLM-as-judge paradigm: it is used in practice and solves the dataset creation problem as a poor man's human judge. However, an ICLR paper documents biases in LLM judges versus humans on dimensions like conciseness and helpfulness. Validation is essential to avoid drifting in biased directions.
